## CHAPTER 11

## Women's Health

## CONTENT OVERVIEW

- Tanner stages
- Breast cancer screening
- Breast mass
- Dysmenorrhea
- Abnormal uterine bleeding
- Endometrial cancer
- Polycystic ovary syndrome
- Contraception
- Cervical cancer screening
- Pelvic exam/abnormal Pap Results
- Vulvovaginitis
- Menopause
- Genitourinary syndrome of menopause
- Osteoporosis screening

## NOTES

<!-- image -->

Joshua Lanclos/APEA

## TANNER STAGES

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

## QUESTION #1

Which of the following patients is at highest risk for developing breast cancer?

1. A 45-year-old female who had six pregnancies
2. A 61-year-old nulliparous female with dense breast tissue
3. A 50-year-old female who has a higher body mass
4. A 32-year-old transgender female on hormone replacement therapy for 2 years

## Breast Cancer: Increased Risk

## Age

Increased estrogen exposure

- Combined hormonal contraceptives (CHC), Hormone Replacement Therapy (HRT)
- Early menarche (<age 12), late menopause (>age 55)
- Nulliparous

## Family history/genetic risk

- Can be estimated using screening tools
- $ BCRAT, Ontario tool
- BRCA 1 & 2 genetic testing: REFER

Lifestyle: alcohol, obesity, smoking, etc.

## Breast Cancer Screening

Females who have average breast cancer risk

| Organization   | Age   | Frequency of Screening Mammogram   |
|----------------|-------|------------------------------------|
| ACS (2023)     | 40-44 | Offer screening                    |
|                | 45-54 | Annually                           |
|                | >55   | Every 1-2 years                    |
| ACOG (2025)    | 40-75 | Q 1-2 years                        |
| USPSTF (2024)  | 40-74 | Q 2 years                          |

Order: Bilateral screening mammogram, 3D (tomosynthesis) preferred

## Breast Masses

- Benign
- $ Fibroadenomas
- $ Cysts
- $ Fibrocystic breasts
- Malignant: mimics benign!
- $ About 9% occur in females <45 years of age
- $ Signs:
- Change in breast size/symmetry
- Change in skin texture
- Nipple inversion or discharge

<!-- image -->

## NOTES

## NOTES Workup for Breast Mass

- Start with a complete history and physical exam.
- Imaging based on age:

| <30 years    | Age 30-39                                       | 40 and older                                          |
|--------------|-------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------|
| · Ultrasound | · Ultrasound or diagnostic mammogram acceptable | · Diagnostic mammogram · Tomosynthesis (3D) preferred |

TIP: These are the INITIAL best tests to order based on age; other diagnostics may be ordered based on initial results.

## Dysmenorrhea

Refers to PAIN associated with menses Primary

- Onset since menarche
- Severity stable
- Improves with parity
- Dyspareunia unusual

Manage in primary care

## Secondary

- Onset mid-20s or older
- Increasing in severity
- Endometriosis, PID, etc.
- Dyspareunia, especially deep Refer to OBGYN

## QUESTION #2

A 28-year-old patient reports progressively worsening menstrual pain after pregnancy 2 years ago. There was no history of menstrual cramping prior to pregnancy. What should be the understanding?

1. This is a normal finding in patients who have previously given birth.
2. Taking an NSAID will eliminate menstrual pain.
3. Symptoms suggest that there may be an underlying structural problem.
4. This pain can be managed with lifestyle modifications.

## Dysmenorrhea Workup

- History
- Physical exam
- $ Rule out abdominal/pelvic abnormalities (secondary causes)
- $ Pelvic exam may be deferred if young, no sexual activity
- Labs: STI, pregnancy, UTI
- Transvaginal ultrasound (or refer): if pathology suspected

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

## Primary Dysmenorrhea Management

- Nonpharmacologic: heat and exercise
- Pharmacologic:
- $ NSAIDs: initiated at onset (or a few days prior) to menses
- $ Hormonal contraceptives
- Combined hormonal contraceptives: pill, patch, ring
- Progestin injections: medroxyprogesterone acetate (Depo-Provera) (q3 months)
- Progestin IUDs: Mirena and Liletta (8 years), Kyleena (5 years), and Skyla (3 years); all release levonorgestrel
- No relief? Not following expected course?
- $ Look for secondary cause and refer!

## Normal Menstrual Cycle

<!-- image -->

© Dee-sign/Shutterstock NOTES

| Hormone                      | Function                        |
|------------------------------|---------------------------------|
| Follicle-stimulating hormone | Follicular growth & development |
| Estrogen                     | Endometrium preparation         |
| Luteinizing hormone          | Liberates the egg               |
| Progesterone                 | Prepares for implantation       |

## NOTES Abnormal Uterine Bleeding (AUB)

<!-- image -->

## AUB-Differential Diagnosis

- Consider differential by age/history.
- Possible causes-PALM-COEIN classification

|                   |    | Cause                  | Consider by AGE:                                                                                                         |
|-------------------|----|------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Structural causes | P  | Polyps                 | >30 years of age                                                                                                         |
| Structural causes | A  | Adenomyosis            | >30 years of age                                                                                                         |
| Structural causes | L  | Leiomyoma/fibroids     | >30 years of age                                                                                                         |
| Structural causes | M  | Malignancy/hyperplasia | Premenopausal with risk factors (obesity, DM, PCOS) or postmenopausal *Must consider in all females of reproductive age! |

May have more than one!

## AUB-Differential Diagnosis

- Consider differential by age/history.
- Possible causes-PALM-COEIN classification

|                      |    | Cause                   | Consider by AGE:   |
|----------------------|----|-------------------------|--------------------|
| Nonstructural causes | C  | Coagulopathy            | Any age            |
| Nonstructural causes | O  | Ovulatory dysfunction   | Any age            |
| Nonstructural causes | E  | Endometrial             | Any age            |
| Nonstructural causes | I  | Iatrogenic, medications | Any age            |
| Nonstructural causes | N  | Not classified          | Any age            |

May have more than one!

## Endometrial Cancer

- AUB is cardinal sign.
- Risks:
- $ Prolonged or increased estrogen
- $ Unopposed estrogen
- $ Chronic anovulation
- Evaluation:
- $ Transvaginal US
- $ Endometrial "stripe" thickness

TIP: Postmenopausal and intermenstrual bleeding is always concerning for endometrial cancer!

## QUESTION #3

A 23-year-old female presents to the clinic with concerns related to irregular menses. She is overweight and reports hirsutism since puberty. Which of the following statements is true?

1. A pelvic ultrasound is required to diagnose PCOS.
2. Fibroids are the most likely diagnosis.
3. An androgen producing tumor is most likely the cause of symptoms.
4. Polycystic ovarian syndrome diagnostic criteria has been met.

## PCOS: Diagnosis

Complex endocrinopathy Pathophysiology is unclear.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

NOTES

## NOTES PCOS Differential Diagnosis

| Differential Diagnosis                            | Characteristic                                                                                                                                          | Workup                                                                         |
|---------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Nonclassic congenital adrenal hyperplasia (NCCAH) | · Hyperandrogenism, oligomenorrhea, polycystic ovaries, possible premature pubarche · Increased risk: Mediterranean, Hispanic, Ashkenazi Jewish females | · 17-hydroxyprogesterone at 8 a.m.                                             |
| Androgen-secreting tumors                         | · Recent onset of severe hirsutism, progressive worsening, signs of virilization · Postmenopausal more common                                           | · Serum testosterone · Serum DHEAS                                             |
| Thyroid disorder, hyperprolactinemia              | · Oligomenorrhea                                                                                                                                        | · TSH · Prolactin level                                                        |
| Cushing syndrome                                  | · Moon facies, facial plethora, supraclavicular fat pads, purple striae                                                                                 | · 24-hour urine: free cortisol and creatinine · Dexamethasone suppression test |

## Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome (PCOS)

Complex endocrinopathy

- 50-70% have insulin resistance.
- Diabetes mellitus
- Metabolic syndrome
- Obesity
- CVD
- Endometrial cancer
- Infertility
- And more!

| Diagnostics to order:   | Diagnostics to order:   |
|-------------------------|-------------------------|
| hCG                     | Lipids                  |
| CBC                     | Glucose/A1C             |
| TSH                     |                         |

<!-- image -->

© Jones & Bartlett Learning

## PCOS Management

## QUESTION #4

In counseling a patient who desires contraception, which advice is accurate?

1. An IUD can be used if the patient has a nulliparous cervix.
2. Combined oral contraceptives may be used if the patient has a history of deep vein thrombosis.
3. Patient must be referred to a specialist to insert long-acting reversible contraceptives.
4. Combined hormonal contraceptives cannot be used if patient is breastfeeding their 9-month-old.

## Contraceptive Selection/Counseling

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

## NOTES

## NOTES CHC Prescribing Tips

| Hormone   | Considerations                                                                                                                                                                               | Adjustment Tips                                                                                                                               |
|-----------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Estrogen  | Ethinylestradiol component Ultra-low dose: <20 mcg Low lose: 20-35 mcg CHCs Highest dose: ≥50 mcg · Assess unacceptable risk · Know when risks outweigh benefits                             | · Increase estrogen dose if: $ Breakthrough bleeding $ Acne or hirsutism · Decrease estrogen dose if $ Nausea $ Breast tenderness $ Headaches |
| Progestin | Androgenic activity: may cause acne, oily skin, hair growth · High: norgestrel, levonorgestrel · Middle: norethindrone · Low: ethynodiol, norgestimate, desogestrel, drospirenone, dienogest | · Norethindrone may reduce breakthrough bleeding · If acne or hirsutism occurs, switch to low- androgen progestin                             |

Note: No longer have "high" dose estrogen, just low, a little higher, and highest

## CHC Contraceptive Risk

CHC known to increase risk for DVT, heart attack, stroke

## Absolute contraindications:

- ≥35 years + smoking 15 cig/day
- CVD risks: hypertension (uncontrolled), ischemic heart disease, valvular heart disease, diabetes (with vascular complications)
- History DVT, PE, stroke, MI
- Migraine with aura
- <3 weeks postpartum
- History of breast/endometrial CA
- Cirrhosis

TIP: If patient is high risk for thromboembolic event = Copper IUD

## Contraceptive Options

<!-- image -->

© elenabsl/Shutterstock

| Method             | Indications                                                                                                               | Contraindications                                                      |
|--------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Copper IUD         | Hx of breast cancer, CKD, cirrhosis, high risk of DVT, multiple risk factors for CVD, postpartum (<10 min after delivery) | Distorted uterine cavity, Unexplained AUB, Untreated PID               |
| Levenorgestrel lUD | Patient preference Postpartum (<10 min after delivery)                                                                    | Distorted uterine cavity Unexplained AUB, Untreated PID, Breast cancer |
| Progestin only     | Patient preference Postpartum with risk factors of DVT (oral option) Breastfeeding                                        | Anticonvulsant use, Rifampin therapy, Bariatric surgery                |
| Depo-Provera       | Breastfeeding                                                                                                             | Breast cancer, Chronic kidney disease                                  |

## Cervical Cancer

Caused by the human papillomavirus (HPV)

- HPV usually clears within 8-24 months (especially if ≤24 years old).
- $ Persistent infection-causes cancer
- High-risk (hrHPV) subtypes
- $ Types 16, 18: 70% HPV-related cancers
- $ 12 other known hrHPV subtypes
- $ Other cancers:
- Oropharynx
- Penis
- Anal
- Cervix
- Vagina, vulva

## HPV Vaccination: Gardasil

- Covers nine of the HPV subtypes (including two strains that commonly cause genital warts!) Immunization schedule:

## Ages 9-14:

- $ 2 doses, given 6-12 months apart

Ages 15-26 or if immunocompromised:

- $ 3 doses, given at 0, 1-2, 6 months

Ages 27-45:

- $ shared decision making

## Cervical Screening Average Risk Patients

Average risk

- Asymptomatic
- Immunocompetent
- Hx of normal screening results (if previously screened)

## Ubiquitous!!!

© Jones & Bartlett Learning

<!-- image -->

## NOTES

## NOTES Age 21-29

- Cytology q3 years
- ACS: initiate age 25 (HPV preferred q5 years)

## Age 30-65

- Cotesting (cytology + HPV) q5 years (preferred)
- Cytology q3 years
- HPV q5 years

## Special Consideration for Cervical Screening

Stop screening if:

- Total hysterectomy (removal of cervix) for benign reasons (no evidence of CIN2, CIN3, A1S, or cervical cancer)
- ≥65 years: if three negative Pap tests or two negative HPV tests in last 10 years

More frequent screening if:

- HIV
- Immunocompromised
- History of cervical cancer
- Exposed to diethylstilbestrol before birth
- Previous abnormal cervical cytology or positive HPV

Patients with abnormal screening results rarely return to average risk screening guidelines.

## Tips for the Pelvic Exam

- Prior to speculum insertion
- $ Apply scant lubrication to finger.
- $ Press down while inserting finger.
- $ Sweep vagina to locate cervix.
- Introital tone: guides speculum selection

<!-- image -->

© MedicalArtInc/iStock

## Proper Pap Collection

Collect cells from TZ & SCJ 360° clockwise rotation **Never reverse direction! Cervix brush: 5 rotations Spatula: 1 rotation Cytobrush: 2-3 rotations

## Cervix brush/broom

© Jones & Bartlett Learning

<!-- image -->

## Management of Abnormal Pap Results

ASCCP Recommendations are based on risks (current results, past history) for developing CIN3+

| Results                    | Action                                                       |
|----------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------|
| Unsatisfactory sample      | Repeat testing ASAP (no more than 4 months)                  |
| CIN 1                      | Observation; repeat cytology in 1 year                       |
| Positive HPV               | Reflex cytology testing IF HPV 16-18: colposcopy with biopsy |
| HPV + ASCUS or higher      | Refer for colposcopy if immunocompromised                    |
| LSIL (HPV pos or neg)      | Refer for colposcopy if immunocompromised                    |
| HSIL (CIN2 or CIN3) or AIS | Refer for excision                                           |

CIN: Cervical intraepithelial neoplasia

AIS: Cervical adenocarcinoma in situ

LSIL: Low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion

HSIL: High-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion

Transformation zone (TZ) Squamocolumnar junction (SCJ)

<!-- image -->

## Spatula followed by Cytobrush

OR

© Jones & Bartlett Learning

<!-- image -->

## QUESTION #5

A 25-year-old patient reports vaginal discharge and itching. Vaginitis is suspected. What should be the understanding?

1. The color and consistency of the discharge will determine the cause.
2. The most likely diagnosis is candidiasis due to the report of discharge.
3. Sexually transmitted diseases are not likely due to the report of itching.
4. Further information is required to determine the etiology.

## Vulvovaginitis

Inflammation causing change in odor or discharge, associated itching and discomfort

- Differential diagnosis
- $ Bacterial vaginosis (BV)
- $ Vulvovaginal candidiasis
- $ Trichomonas vaginalis infection
- $ Other STIs causing cervicitis and discharge

Self-diagnosis often inaccurate!

## Vulvovaginitis Assessment

| DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS    | DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS - Bacterial Vaginosis                     | DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS - Vulvovaginal Candidiasis                           | DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS - Trichomoniasis                                       |
|---------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Patients most susceptible | Multiple partners, no condoms, douching, HSV-2 infection         | Pregnancy, CHC use, diabetes, weakened immune system, recent antibiotic use | Multiple sex partners, no condom use, HIV infection, teens, and older females |
| Organisms                 | Aerobe overgrowth                                                | Candida albicans                                                            | Trichomonas vaginalis                                                         |
| Discharge                 | Thin, milky, malodorous Coats walls of vagina                    | Thick, cheesy or curd-like, white or yellow                                 | Malodorous, yellow-green, copious, frothy                                     |
| Vaginal pH                | >4.5 (elevated)                                                  | <4.5 (normal)                                                               | >4.5 (elevated)                                                               |
| Testing                   | Positive KOH whiff test                                          | NAAT                                                                        | NAAT                                                                          |
| Microscopy                | Clue cells                                                       | Buds, hyphae, with KOH                                                      | Trichomonads                                                                  |
| Treatment                 | Metronidazole PO 500 mg BID ×7 days or vaginal gel daily ×5 days | Vaginal-azole cream or ovule (suppository); fluconazole 150 mg PO once      | Metronidazole 500 mg PO BID ×7 days                                           |

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

## QUESTION #6

A patient has a diagnosis of vulvovaginal candidiasis. This is the patient's third episode of candidiasis in 4 months. Which of the following should be recommended?

1. The patient can douche to help prevent future episodes.
2. The patient should abstain from sexual contact for 2 months.
3. The patient should be screened for immunocompromising conditions.
4. The patient should have their Mirena IUD removed.

## Perimenopause

Body's transition to menopause:

- Mean length 4 years; median duration 7-10 years!
- Starts at different ages (as early as mid-30s!)
- Low estrogen states: hormonal testing not useful

## Symptoms

- Irregular menses
- Cognitive changes ("Brain Fog")
- Sleep/mood changes
- Hot flashes and night sweats
- Osteoporosis risk
- Cardiovascular risk

## Menopausal Management

Hormone replacement therapy (first-line)

- COC: perimenopause and desire contraception
- Estrogen only: total hysterectomy
- Estrogen + Progestin: if uterus present
- Contraindications: same as CHC

Nonhormonal therapy (useful for contraindications/patient wishes)

- FDA approved:
- $ Paroxetine (Brisdelle) 7.5 mg daily
- $ Fezolinetant 45 mg daily
- Off-label: Supported by the North American Menopause Society
- $ SSRIs: citalopram, escitalopram
- $ SNRIs: desvenlafaxine, venlafaxine
- $ Gabapentinoids: gabapentin

TIP: Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest amount of time for symptoms.

<!-- image -->

## Genitourinary symptoms

- Vaginal dryness
- Dyspareunia
- Urinary urgency
- Urinary frequency
- Recurrent UTIs

## NOTES

## NOTES Genitourinary Syndrome of Menopause (Vulvovaginal Atrophy)

- Low-estrogen state
- Assessment
- $ Pale, dry, smooth, and shiny epithelium with loss of vaginal rugae
- $ Tissue fragility/petechiae
- $ Vulvovaginal dryness
- $ Abnormal discharge
- $ Vaginal pH >5

© KAMAKSI/Shutterstock

<!-- image -->

## Vulvovaginal Atrophy (VVA) Management

- Vaginal moisturizers/lubricants
- Topical (vaginal) estrogen: cream, tablets, ring, capsule $ Preferred to systemic if only VVA symptoms
- Ospemifene: oral
- $ Common selective estrogen receptor modulator SE = hot flashes
- Vaginal DHEA (prasterone): inserted daily

## QUESTION #7

An Asian female patient asks about their risk factors for osteoporosis. What should be the response?

1. "Your sex and ethnicity mean you have a lower risk for osteoporosis."
2. "Drinking three glasses of wine per week increases your risk."
3. "Your history of having a spontaneous fracture puts you at higher risk."
4. "Your current weight of 120 pounds is protective against osteoporosis."

<!-- image -->

## Bone Health

- Calcium
- $ Ensure sufficient intake (≥1,200 mg daily)
- Vitamin D
- $ Ensure sufficient intake (800-1,000 IU daily)
- $ Supplement with vitamin D3 (cholecalciferol)
- Modifiable risk factors for osteoporosis
- $ Reduce smoking, alcohol, medications/oral steroids
- $ Weight-bearing, balance, and resistance exercises
- $ Fall prevention

## Osteoporosis Screening

Risk factors

- Advanced age
- Previous fragility fracture
- Low body weight
- Parental history of hip fracture
- Rheumatoid arthritis
- Cigarette smoking
- Excess alcohol intake
- Early menopause
- Long-term glucocorticoid therapy

Risk factor assessment (FRAX tool)

- 10-year probability of osteoporotic fracture

## Screening: DEXA scan (Gold standard)

- Females ≥65 years old
- Females/males at any age with risk factors

## Osteoporosis Diagnosis & Management

| Osteopenia   | T-Score -1.0 to -2.5   |
|--------------|------------------------|
| Osteoporosis | T-Score <-2.5          |

Who needs pharmacologic therapy?

1. Osteopenia + increased FRAX score
2. Osteopenia + Hx of fragility fracture
3. Osteoporosis

## First-line: bisphosphonates

- Alendronate (Fosamax)
- Risedronate (Actonel, Atelvia)
- Ibandronate (Boniva)
- Zoledronic acid (Reclast)

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

NOTES

## NOTES

## QUESTION #8

Which of the following conditions is not a contraindication for prescribing alendronate?

1. History of bariatric surgery
2. Hypocalcemia
3. Postmenopausal
4. Barrett esophagus

## Osteoporosis Management

## ALTERNATIVES

Denosumab (Prolia): monoclonal antibody

- Intolerant or unresponsive to bisphosphonates
- BMD decreases rapidly when dc'd.
- $ MUST start another medication ASAP
- Postmenopausal women not candidates for denosumab or bisphosphonate

Raloxifene: Selective Estrogen Receptor Modulator (SERM)

## Osteoporosis Evaluation

Typical duration of tx:

| Oral   | 5 years   |
|--------|-----------|
| IV     | 3 years   |

Follow-up DEXA individualized. Consider if:

1. Clearly defined objectives
2. Results will influence patient management.

## EXAMPLES:

- New risk factors/new fracture
- Prior to cessation of bisphosphonate therapy

## Resources

- Apps
- $ CDC Contraception App: "Contraception"
- $ Cervical Cancer Screening App: "ASCCP Management Guidelines" ($10)
- $ STI Treatment App: "STI Tx Guide"
- $ USPSTF Recommendations App
- $ John Hopkins Menopause Guide App
- Websites
- $ Fracture Risk Assessment Tool (FRAX)
- $ American Cancer Society on Breast Cancer
- $ NIH Breast Cancer Risk Assessment Tool
- $ United States Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF)

<!-- image -->

## EXAM CHECKLIST

- Dysmenorrhea
- Abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB)
- Amenorrhea, polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)
- Contraception
- Cervical cancer screening
- Ovarian mass
- Vulvovaginitis
- Osteoporosis
- Breast mass
- Nipple discharge
- Know clinical presentation (subjective, objective findings)
- Know how to diagnose
- What's in differential diagnosis?
- Pharmacologic, nonpharmacologic management
- Follow-up care
- Recognize normal course
- Recognize complications

<!-- image -->
